title: The serpent who came to teach
hookLine: a tiny snake falls into a praying woman's hands and grows up to teach yoga's eight limbs
carry: eight limbs, and ethics come first
last: VIVEKA: TELLING THE SELF FROM WHAT IT SEES — INDRA GOES BACK.

lines: A WOMAN OFFERS WATER TO THE SUN.
A TINY SNAKE FALLS INTO HER HANDS.
cards: A woman named Gonika stands at a river at sunrise, offering water to the sun from her cupped hands. For years she has prayed for someone to pass her learning on to.

As she lifts her hands, something tiny drops into them: a little snake. It becomes a child. A traditional story, still told in yoga schools, says this was Shesha, the great serpent Vishnu rests on, come down to teach.
Fallen, pata, into folded hands, anjali. Patanjali.

teach.h: A SAGE WITH A SERPENT'S COIL.
teach.b: That's why statues of Patanjali often show a sage whose lower body is a serpent's coil, with hoods spread over his head.
Many yoga classes still open with an old verse that bows to him with folded hands, the sage who cleared the mind with yoga, speech with grammar and the body with medicine.

Many teachers read the story as a picture of how Hindus hold this book: yoga as a gift that came down to clean a person all the way through. So what did he teach? Sutra 2.29 lists the eight limbs, ashtanga.
Yama, the restraints: how you treat others. Niyama, the observances: how you keep yourself. Asana, the seat.
Pranayama, the breath. Pratyahara, the senses drawing back. Dharana, concentration.
Dhyana, meditation. Samadhi, absorption. Listen to the direction.

It starts with other people and moves inward, until only the object shines. Teachers read the shape two ways: a ladder, ethics first and then body and mind; or limbs, which grow together, like a child's arms and legs.
Either way, the proportion is plain. Ethics first, twice.
Posture, one word out of eight.

So when a studio timetable says Ashtanga, six p.m., bring water, that class is a modern tradition of its own. The word behind it is older, and in the sutra it begins with how you treat the people in the room.

how: Many yoga classes open with a chant bowing to Patanjali, often pictured with a serpent's coil and hoods; classical teaching presents the eight limbs of 2.29 as the framework of the whole practice, starting with the restraints and observances.

o: eight breathing methods done in a fixed order
a set of eight rules for diet and sleep
the eight limbs of yoga, from ethics to absorption

games.q: the teacher and his eight limbs — tap the pairs.

s: ashtanga in the sutras means a vigorous posture class
the class is a modern tradition. in 2.29, ashtanga is eight limbs, and only one is a posture.
the list moves from other people inward to absorption
yama and niyama come first; dharana, dhyana and samadhi last.
in a traditional story, Patanjali is the serpent Shesha come down to teach
he falls as a tiny snake into Gonika's cupped hands as she offers water to the sun.

games.q: a friend says, I want to start yoga. which limb does Patanjali's list begin with?
games.why: 2.29 begins with yama, the restraints, starting with non-harm. posture is third.

practice: Walk the eight in miniature: a moment of goodwill toward someone, contentment with this exact moment, a steady and easy seat, a slightly longer breath, sounds and sights left in the background.
Then rest your attention on one point, maybe the breath at the nostrils, let it flow without breaks, and if the point fills everything, let it. If it doesn't, that's normal.

wordCard.voice: Ashtanga. The eight parts of yoga in sutra 2.29, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption.

orig.note: Sanskrit aṣṭāṅga: aṣṭa (eight) plus aṅga (limb, part); the eight limbs of yoga in 2.29.

carryVoice: Your line: eight limbs, and ethics come first. The serpent came down to teach all eight, not just the poses. Day four hundred fifty-seven, done.
